---
title: "Crashes, Drawdowns & Nameable Events"
subtitle: "Putting dates and names on the left tail"
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, BAND, despine, mark_event
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
R = datasets.load_returns()
BANKS = ["JPM", "BAC", "C", "WFC", "GS"]
```

A **crash** is not a special object in the data — it is simply a day deep in the
**left tail**.  The previous page showed those tails are fat; this page walks over
to them and reads the dates.  It turns out the worst days have names you'll
recognise.

---

## 1 · The Worst Days Have Names

Average the five banks into one series and ask for its worst days.  They bunch
into two episodes — the **2008–09 financial crisis** and the **March-2020 COVID
crash**:

```{python}
bank_avg = R[BANKS].mean(axis=1)
worst = bank_avg.sort_values().head(5)
print("five worst average-bank days:")
for d, v in worst.items():
    print(f"  {d.date()}   {v:+.1%}")
```

But deep left-tail days are not confined to those two windows.  Nameable crashes
recur across the whole period — each tied to a vote, a downgrade, a pandemic, a
policy shock — and the figure marks five of them, well spread across nineteen
years.

```{python}
#| label: fig-events
#| fig-cap: "Average bank return, 2007–2025, with five nameable crashes marked: Lehman Brothers' collapse (2008-09-15, −15%), the US credit-rating downgrade (2011-08-08, −13%), the Brexit vote (2016-06-24, −7%), the COVID crash (2020-03-16, −17%), and the 2025 'Liberation Day' tariff shock (2025-04-03, −10%). The very deepest days of all sit in the dense 2008–09 cluster on the left."
events = {
    pd.Timestamp("2008-09-15"): "Lehman",
    pd.Timestamp("2011-08-08"): "US downgrade",
    pd.Timestamp("2016-06-24"): "Brexit",
    pd.Timestamp("2020-03-16"): "COVID crash",
    pd.Timestamp("2025-04-03"): "Tariff crash",
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.2, 4.4))
ax.plot(bank_avg.index, bank_avg, color=COOL, lw=0.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.7)
for i, (d, name) in enumerate(events.items()):
    mark_event(ax, d, name, top=0.97 - 0.12 * (i % 2))   # stagger bubbles
ax.set_ylabel("average bank daily return"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("The left tail, with names attached", fontsize=12)
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The five marked events, with sources:

- **Lehman Brothers' bankruptcy** — 2008-09-15 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_Lehman_Brothers))
- **Black Monday 2011**, after S&P's US credit-rating downgrade — 2011-08-08 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Monday_%282011%29))
- **Brexit referendum result** — 2016-06-24 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum))
- **COVID-19 crash** — 2020-03-16 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash))
- **"Liberation Day" tariff crash** — 2025-04-03 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_stock_market_crash))

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## A Crash Is a Quantile, Not a Category
There is no switch in the data that flips to "crash."  We *define* one — say, a day
below the 5th percentile — and the definition is a dial.  Keep that in mind on the
next page, where the same dial moves a co-crash headline from 3% to 67%.
:::

## 2 · Drawdown: the Pain of Staying Invested

A single bad day is one thing; the **drawdown** is the cumulative wound — how far
below its previous peak an investment has fallen, and *for how long*.  Reconstruct
JPM's equity curve and shade the **underwater** region between the running peak and
the price.  The depth is brutal — but the recovery is the real point, and not every
bank got one.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drawdown
#| fig-cap: "Top: JPM equity curve (indexed to 100) with its running peak. Bottom: the drawdown — percent below the prior peak. JPM's worst, −68%, bottoms on 2009-03-09 in the depths of the crisis, then claws back to new highs by 2013 (the shaded region returns to zero). Citigroup's drawdown (dark line) is the other story: −98% at the trough, and nineteen years later still some −69% below its 2007 peak — a wound that never healed."
eq = 100 * np.exp(R["JPM"].cumsum())
peak = eq.cummax()
dd = eq / peak - 1.0
trough = dd.idxmin()
eq_c = 100 * np.exp(R["C"].cumsum())          # Citigroup, for contrast
dd_c = eq_c / eq_c.cummax() - 1.0

fig, (axT, axB) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9.2, 5.4), sharex=True,
                               height_ratios=[2, 1])
axT.plot(eq.index, eq, color=COOL, lw=1.2, label="JPM (indexed to 100)")
axT.plot(peak.index, peak, color=INK, lw=0.9, ls="--", label="running peak")
axT.set_ylabel("price"); axT.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
axT.set_title("Equity curve and its drawdown", fontsize=12); despine(axT)

axB.fill_between(dd.index, dd * 100, 0, color=CRASH, alpha=0.30)
axB.plot(dd_c.index, dd_c * 100, color=INK, lw=1.0)
axB.axvline(trough, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls=":")
# label the two curves inline, in the calm 2013–16 gap, to avoid a box on the line
axB.text(pd.Timestamp("2014-06-01"), -16, "JPM", color=CRASH,
         fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
axB.text(pd.Timestamp("2014-06-01"), -72, "Citigroup", color=INK,
         fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
axB.annotate(f"JPM max drawdown {dd.min():.0%}\n{trough.date()}",
             (trough, dd.min() * 100), textcoords="offset points",
             xytext=(12, 12), fontsize=9, color=INK)
axB.set_ylabel("drawdown (%)"); axB.set_xlabel("date"); despine(axB)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Drawdown has two dimensions — **depth** and **duration**.  JPM's was deep but
temporary.  Citigroup's was near-total and, after the dilution and a 1-for-10
reverse split that the crisis forced, effectively permanent: an investor who held
from 2007 has still not seen their money back.  Same sector, same crash, opposite
endings.

## 3 · The Same Days, Seen in the Distribution

Crashes and the histogram are two views of one thing.  Mark the worst days back on
the return distribution and they land exactly where the **left tail** is shaded —
the fat tail of the last page is *made of* these named days.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tail-marks
#| fig-cap: "Zoomed into the left tail — the bulk of days sits off the right edge, near zero. Bars count how many days landed at each return; the worst 5% (below −3.2%) are shaded. The five named crashes (dashed, labelled) each fall among real, if rare, tail days. They are residents of the fat tail, not outliers off the chart."
x = bank_avg.to_numpy()
cut = np.quantile(x, 0.05)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.8, 4.2))
bins = np.arange(x.min() - 0.003, 0.0, 0.004)   # 0.4%-wide bins resolve the tail
ax.hist(x, bins=bins, color=BAND, alpha=0.85)
ax.axvspan(x.min() - 0.01, cut, color=CRASH, alpha=0.15, label="worst 5% of days")
for d, name in events.items():
    xpos = bank_avg[d]
    ax.axvline(xpos, color=CRASH, lw=1.0, ls="--")
    ax.annotate(name, (xpos, 26), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8,
                color=CRASH, rotation=90)
ax.set_xlim(x.min() - 0.01, -0.02)              # zoom: just the left tail
ax.set_ylim(0, 55)
ax.set_xlabel("average bank daily return"); ax.set_ylabel("days")
ax.set_title("Inside the worst 5%: the named crashes have company", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Takeaway
"Crash" = deep left-tail day; "drawdown" = cumulative distance below the peak.
Both are everyday consequences of fat tails — and on the next page we'll see the
banks don't take these days *alone*.
:::
